content: 1. The characteristics and understanding of antiretroviral therapy (ART) drugs can influence the willingness of individuals to accept pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Comprehensive prevention strategies should be recommended within the community of men who have sex with men (MSM). 2. A national online survey was conducted to assess the response of HIV-negative American MSM to the first efficacy data on PrEP, both before and after the publication of the iPrEx study. MSM members of a large sexual and social networking site were invited to complete surveys in September-October 2010 and January 2011. Chi-square tests were used to compare attitudes before and after the release of the iPrEx results. 3. Before the iPrEx publication, 458 MSM responded to the survey, and after the publication, 4,325 participated. The median age of respondents was 40 years. More than 80% of participants in both survey waves indicated they did not believe they would reduce condom use during anal sex while taking PrEP. However, a significant proportion of high-risk MSM were unfamiliar with PrEP. 4. Programs aimed at educating healthcare providers on risk assessment are necessary to ensure that chemoprophylaxis has a meaningful impact on reducing HIV transmission among MSM. Utilizing sexual and social networking sites to educate at-risk MSM about PrEP could promote its appropriate use. 5. The iPrEx study, published in November 2010, demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV infections among MSM who took daily tenofovir/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC). However, concerns about risk compensation, where individuals might engage in riskier behaviors due to perceived protection, could undermine the benefits of PrEP. 6. An online survey conducted among U.S. MSM recruited from Facebook and Black Gay Chat assessed risk practices and perceptions with and without TDF/FTC. Among 1,155 HIV-negative MSM respondents, 7% anticipated reduced condom use with PrEP, while 75% expected no change. However, 21% perceived a lower risk of HIV infection from unprotected insertive anal sex (UAI) with PrEP, and 39% perceived reduced risk from unprotected receptive anal sex (UAR). 7. While most respondents did not anticipate changing their risk behaviors on PrEP, a substantial minority might adjust their practices, potentially offsetting the benefits. It is crucial to educate MSM populations about PrEP's partial efficacy and provide ongoing risk reduction counseling. 8. A study in Lima, Peru, investigated the willingness of high-risk MSM to use PrEP as an HIV prevention strategy. Factors such as age and education were not independently associated with willingness to use PrEP. Understanding the concerns and fears of the target population is essential before implementing PrEP as an intervention. 9. Following the release of iPrEx results, a survey of North American MSM using an internet social network revealed that 75% expressed interest in using PrEP. However, 20% anticipated decreased condom use for insertive anal sex, and 14% for receptive anal sex. Interventions to minimize risk compensation are warranted. 10. A global online survey of gay and other MSM in the Global South and Global North highlighted disparities in PrEP knowledge and access to HIV-related services. Respondents from the Global South reported lower PrEP knowledge but higher acceptability compared to those from the Global North. Implementation planning for PrEP should address social and structural barriers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. 11. A community survey conducted by the AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) found that while 79% of respondents were willing to take a daily pill that was over 90% effective at preventing HIV, acceptability decreased to 69% when monthly HIV/STD testing was required. Only 41% were willing to take PrEP if a $60 co-pay was involved. Real-life conditions, such as costs and required medical visits, significantly impact PrEP acceptability. 12. A street-intercept survey during New York City's 2011 Gay Pride events revealed that many MSM were unaware of PrEP. Men who believed PrEP had significant side effects were the least likely to consider using it. Efforts to educate MSM about PrEP and address misconceptions are necessary. 13. A global multilingual survey of MSM found that 53% and 60% of respondents had no knowledge of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and PrEP, respectively. However, 70% and 74% expressed strong interest in using PEP and PrEP to prevent HIV. Disseminating information about these prevention tools is strongly needed. 14. MSM in Latin America, Spain, and Portugal using an internet social networking site demonstrated limited awareness but high interest in PrEP. International efforts to increase awareness and access to PrEP are essential to reduce HIV acquisition among at-risk populations.
